segments.text: Procedures and functions: named P L S Q L blocks, stored in the database.
So far, our P L S Q L has lived in anonymous blocks: DECLARE, BEGIN, EXCEPTION, END. A block runs once, and then it is gone. Nothing is stored.
Give the code a name, and it becomes a subprogram, stored in the database and compiled once. Every application can call it, and you share it with GRANT EXECUTE.
Here is a stored procedure, enrol student. CREATE OR REPLACE stores it, compiled, in your schema.
Its first two parameters are IN: the student and the course, which it can only read. The third, p message, is OUT: the procedure writes it, and the caller gets it back.
Parameter types have no length. The body inserts the enrolment, then sets the message.
To call it from a block, declare a variable for the message, and pass it as the third argument.
In a script, EXEC does the same in one line, with a bind variable.
The enrolment table gains a row: student S zero three in course C twenty, with no grade yet. And the variable now holds the message.
Now run the same call a second time. The INSERT repeats the primary key, so Oracle raises dup val on index.
Instead of crashing, execution jumps to the EXCEPTION section. The handler for that error sets a different message.
The caller gets a clear answer, and the table is unchanged.
A function returns a value. Letter grade takes a grade and returns a letter: A from nine, B from seven, C from five, otherwise F.
Because it returns a SQL type, you can call it inside a query, just like a built-in function.
Each enrolment gets its letter. Eight point five is a B, nine is an A, and the new row, with no grade, gets a dash.
Think of a procedure as a vending machine. You put in a coin and a choice, it does something, and it may hand back change through its OUT parameters.
A function is a calculator: numbers in, one answer out, ready to use inside a bigger expression, even a SELECT.
Want an action? Write a procedure. Want a value? Write a function.
As your code grows, group related procedures and functions in a package.
The specification is the menu that callers see. The body is the kitchen, where the code lives.
Callers write the package name, a dot, and the subprogram.
Practise it in the SQL section of the course site.
